choose to be tested; scientists actively design severe tests.","Evolution has no goal of 'truth'; science explicitly aims at truth (even if asymptotically)."],"overturn_conditions":["If the universe is shown to be non-uniform such that past severity guarantees nothing about future structure.","If it is proven that acting on corroboration inevitably requires an unconscious inductive leap."],"shared_structure":["Selection occurs based on past performance (survival/tests) without guarantee of future success.","The mechanism is retrospective (filtering failures) rather than prospective (predicting winners).","Preference for the 'fittest' or 'best-tested' is a heuristic for potential, not a proof of outcome."],"source_memory_refs":["biological_evolution_by_natural_selection"],"transfer_claims":["Just as we bet on the fittest organism without knowing the future environment, we bet on the best-corroborated theory without knowing the next test.","The rationality of the bet lies in the rigor of the filtering process, not in the probability of the winner."]},"claim":"Popper's preference for better-corroborated theories is defensible on his own terms as a non-inductive, methodological rule of 'risk-taking' rather than a probabilistic inference, but accepting this defense costs the scientist any claim that their choice is 'likely true' or rationally superior in terms of expected utility, reducing scientific progress to a gamble on boldness without epistemic security.","counterconditions":[{"case":"If the preference for corroborated theories implicitly assumes the future will resemble the past (uniformity of nature), then it smuggles in (per Tich\u00fd/Miller), then the defense collapses.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If scientists act on corroboration because they believe the theory is 'more likely true,' then reconstructs Popper's distinction between 'logical probability' (which remains low for highly testable theories) and 'methodological preference' (which favors severity). It posits that choosing the best-corroborated theory is akin to a gambler choosing the horse with the most rigorous past performance not because it will win (induction), but because it offers the highest potential payoff (truth-content) if it survives the next test.
